rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception for those who believe and do good is glossed as people who recited the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: ثم رددناه أسفل سافلين إلا الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding proof, the revival of dead earth by rain is presented as another proof of resurrection.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر سبحانه دلالة أخرى على البعث فقال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains the earth as dead; the author also glosses it as dry and worn bare of vegetation.
rows.anchor: يعني هالكة عن مجاهد أي يابسة دارسة من أثر النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water sent down upon the earth is rain.
rows.anchor: وهو المطر { اهتزت } أي تحركت بالنبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth moves as vegetation grows; the word denotes vigorous movement in every direction.
rows.anchor: والاهتزاز شدة الحركة في الجهات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It grew” means the earth increased and multiplied its vegetation.
rows.anchor: أي زادت أي أضعفت نباتها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan offers the alternative that the earth swells as its vegetation appears.
rows.anchor: وقيل: انتفخت لظهور نباتها عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Every pair” means every kind, and “delightful” means pleasing to the eye in its beautiful appearance and color.
rows.anchor: من كل زوج } أي من كل صنف { بهيج } مؤنق للعين حسن الصورة واللون

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ cites the construction “inna Zaydan innahu la-qāʾim” and reports that the verse’s doubled “inna” construction works in this relative-clause setting.
rows.anchor: وزعم الفراء أن قولك إن زيدا إنه لقائم وروي أن هذه الآية إنما صلحت في الذي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj rejects a restriction to relative clauses: the doubled “anna” construction is sound with other nouns too.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: لا فرق بين الذي وغيره في باب أن أن قلت أن زيدا أنه قائم كان جيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Likewise” compares this revelation to the Qur’anic signs already mentioned; the signs are clear proofs of oneness, justice, and religious laws.
rows.anchor: أي ومثل ما تقدم من آيات القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revealed the signs and guides to religion whoever He wills.
rows.anchor: أي أنزلنا الله يهدي إلى الدين من يريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported explanations take the guidance as guidance to prophethood, to reward, or to guidance for whoever follows its direction.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إلى النبوة. وقيل: إلى الثواب. وقيل: يهدي من يهتدي بهداه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who believe are believers in Muhammad; “those who Judaized” are the Jews, followed by the Sabians, Christians, Magians, and polytheists.
rows.anchor: بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At resurrection God distinguishes the true party from the false, making the soundness of truth known: the truthful are bright-faced and the falsehood-followers dark-faced.
rows.anchor: أي يبين المحق من المبطل بما يضطر إلى العلم بصحة الصحيح فيبيض وجه المحق ويسود وجه المبطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Deciding between them” means distinguishing truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: والفصل التمييز بين الحق والباطل

words: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ شَهِيدٌ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is fully aware of everything that can be witnessed, knowing it before it comes to be; He knows the unseen.
rows.anchor: أي عليم مطلع على ما من شأنه أن يشاهد بعلمه قبل أن يكون لأنه علام الغيوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is addressed, while all morally responsible people are intended; “Have you not seen?” means “Have you not known?”
rows.anchor: ثم خاطب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم والمراد به جميع المكلفين فقال

words: يَسْجُدُ لَهُۥ مَن فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَن فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rational beings in the heavens and earth prostrate to God; the sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, and animals also prostrate through submission and compliance with their Creator.
rows.anchor: وصف سبحانه هذه الأشياء بالسجود وهو الخضوع والذل والانقياد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The many people who prostrate are believers; the sentence then restarts with the many for whom punishment is decreed.
rows.anchor: يعني المؤمنين الذين يسجدون لله تعالى وانقطع ذكر الساجدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those punished are people who refuse to prostrate and do not affirm God’s oneness.
rows.anchor: أي ممن أبى السجود ولا يوحده سبحانه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the punishment clause implies “many refused to prostrate,” since punishment is deserved only through abandoning prostration.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: قوله وكثير حق عليه العذاب يدل على أن المعنى وكثير أبى السجود

words: وَمَن يُهِنِ ٱللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُۥ مِن مُّكْرِمٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever God makes wretched and sends to Hell has no one to honor him with happiness and Paradise, since God alone controls punishment and reward.
rows.anchor: بأن يشقيه ويدخله جهنم فما له من مكرم بالسعادة أي بإدخاله الجنة لأنه لا يملك العقوبة والمثوبة سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does as He wills, granting favor to or taking vengeance on both believers and unbelievers.
rows.anchor: من الإنعام والانتقام بالفريقين من المؤمنين والكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Prophet migrated, this Medinan verse was revealed; the author calls it the first verse revealed about fighting.
rows.anchor: حتى هاجر فأنزل الله عليه هذه الآية بالمدينة وهي أول آية نزلت في القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse has an ellipsis: believers were permitted to fight, or permission to fight was granted because they had been wronged by expulsion and abuse.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية محذوف وتقديره أذن للمؤمنين أن يقاتلوا أو بالقتال من أجل أنهم ظلموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement is a promise that God will give the believers victory.
rows.anchor: وهذا وعد لهم بالنصر معناه أنه سينصرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possibility is that the expelled believers went to Medina, making the verse Medinan.
rows.anchor: يحتمل معناه أن يكون أراد أخرجوا إلى المدينة فتكون الآية مدنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the expulsion was to Abyssinia, which would make the verse Meccan; persecution forced them to leave.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل إلى الحبشة فتكون الآية مكية وذلك بأنهم تعرضوا لهم بالأذى حتى اضطروا إلى الخروج

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī explains “without right” as meaning they had done nothing to deserve expulsion.
rows.anchor: وقوله بغير حق معناه من غير أن استحقوا ذلك عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were expelled solely because they professed that God alone is their Lord.
rows.anchor: أي لم يخرجوا من ديارهم إلى لقولهم ربنا الله وحده

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar says the verse was revealed about the Emigrants and also applies to the family of Muhammad, who were expelled and intimidated.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر ع: نزلت في المهاجرين وجرت في آل محمد عليهم السلام

words: وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلنَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to his earlier discussion of God’s repelling some people by means of others.
rows.anchor: قد تقدم الكلام في هذا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj assigns monasteries to Jesus’ dispensation, churches to Moses’ dispensation, and mosques to Muhammad’s; without divine restraint, prayer places in every dispensation would be demolished.
rows.anchor: عن الزجاج، والمعنى ولولا أن دفع الله بعض الناس ببعض لهدم في كل شريعة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says churches are in villages, monasteries in mountains and deserts and shared by three communities, mosques belong to Muslims, and ṣalawāt are Jewish synagogues.
rows.anchor: وقيل: البيع للنصارى في القرى والصوامع في الجبال والبراري ويشترك فيها الفرق الثلاث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Qatāda identify ṣalawāt as Jewish synagogues, whose name was Arabized from their term ṣalawt.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة: الصلوات كنائس اليهود يسمونها صلوة فعربت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan takes ṣalawāt to mean the prayer itself, destroyed by killing those who perform it or preventing them from praying.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: أراد بذلك عين الصلاة وهدم الصلاة بقتل فاعليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes ṣalawāt as prayer places, as in the command not to approach prayer while intoxicated, meaning mosques.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد بالصلوات المصليات كما قال: لا تقربوا الصلاة وأنتم سكارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “in them” may refer only to mosques, or to all the previously named worship places, where God is generally remembered.
rows.anchor: الهاء تعود إلى المساجد. وقيل: إلى جميع المواضع التي تقدمت لأن الغالب فيها ذكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises to support whoever supports His religion and religious law.
rows.anchor: هذا وعد من الله بأنه سينصر من ينصر دينه وشريعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Strong, mighty” means powerful and overwhelming.
rows.anchor: إن لقوي عزيز } أي قادر قاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God first brought people to life after they were lifeless sperm, then causes them to die at the end of their appointed lifetimes, then revives them for resurrection and judgment.
rows.anchor: بعد أن كنتم نطفا ميتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one able to originate life is able to restore it.
rows.anchor: وفيه بيان أن من قدر على ابتداء الأحياء قدر على إعادة الأحياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The human is ungrateful” means stubbornly denying the Creator despite the evidence for creation.
rows.anchor: أي جحود فإنه مع هذه الأدلة الدالة على الخلق يجحد الخالق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says each community or past generation was given a religious law that its people practice.
rows.anchor: أي شريعة هم عاملون بها عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations take mansak as a familiar worship place or place of worship, including the pilgrimage sites.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مكانا يألفونه وموضعا يعتادونه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda explain mansak as a place for sacrifice, whether at Mina or elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقيل: موضع قربان أي متعبد في إراقة الدماء مني أو غيره عن مجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is explained either as forbidding the opponents to dispute with the Prophet, or as addressed to him because a dispute is mutual.
rows.anchor: هذا نهي لهم عن منازعة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم. وقيل: نهي له لأن المنازعة تكون من اثنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their dispute concerned why Muslims eat animals they slaughter but refuse animals God “killed,” meaning carrion; the instruction is not to quarrel over slaughter.
rows.anchor: ومنازعتهم قولهم أتأكلون ما قتلتم ولا تأكلون ما قتله الله يعنون الميتة أي فلا يخاصمنك في أمر الذبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that opponents have no right to contest the Prophet’s law, which has abrogated the earlier laws.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه ليس لهم أن ينازعوك في شريعتهم وقد نسخت هذه الشريعة الشرائع المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should disregard their quarrelling and call people to God’s oneness and religion.
rows.anchor: أي لا تلتفت إلى منازعتك وادع إلى توحيد ربك وإلى دينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being on straight guidance means following an upright religion.
rows.anchor: إنك لعلى هدى مستقيم } أي على دين قيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they argue about slaughter, the Prophet should say God knows their denial and will repay them; this was before the command to fight.
rows.anchor: أي إن خاصموك في أمر الذبيحة فقل الله أعلم بتكذيبكم فهو يجازيكم به وهذا قبل الأمر بالقتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view concerns argumentative obstruction after the proof is established: do not debate in that manner, but answer with this statement.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه إن جادلوك على سبيل المراء والتعنت بعد لزوم الحجة فلا تجادلهم على هذا الوجه وادفعهم بهذا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation applies the argument to abrogation of religious laws and says to refer the dispute to God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه وإن نازعوك في نسخ الشريعة فحاكمهم إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Day of Resurrection, God will decide between them by distinguishing their disagreements.
rows.anchor: أي: يفصل بينكم { فيما كنتم فيه تختلفون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is addressed, but all morally responsible people are intended by the statement.
rows.anchor: ثم قال لنبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم والمراد جميع المكلفين

words: أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows everything, small or great, in heaven and earth; nothing is hidden from Him.
rows.anchor: من قليل وكثير لا يخفى عليه شيء من ذلك

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says all this knowledge is recorded in the Preserved Book.
rows.anchor: أي مثبت في الكتاب المحفوظ عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Writing in the Preserved Tablet is easy for God and requires no lines or letters; He only says “Be,” and it is. Another view says His judgment is easy.
rows.anchor: أي كتابته في اللوح المحفوظ على الله يسير لا يحتاج إلى معالجة خطوط وحروف وإنما يقول كن فيكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says God deserves exaltation because He is eternal, without beginning or end; baraka derives from firmness and stability.
rows.anchor: استحق التعظيم بأنه قديم لم يزل ولا يزال لأنه مأخوذ من البروك الذي هو الثبوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the best creator because His creation has no defect; khalq originally means measuring, as when leather is measured before cutting.
rows.anchor: وقال أحسن الخالقين لأنه لا تفاوت في خلقه وأصل الخلق التقدير، يقال خلقت الأديم

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Ḥudhayfa says, “You make things and God makes things, and He is the best of makers.”
rows.anchor: وقال حذيفة في هذه الآية تصنعون ويصنع الله وهو خير الصانعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shows that “creating” may be attributed to beings other than God, though creation in its true sense belongs only to God.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دليل على أن اسم الخلق قد يطلق على فعل غير الله تعالى إلا أن الحقيقة في الخلق لله سبحانه فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True creation is bringing something into existence with exact measure and no disparity, as supported by the verse “His are creation and command.”
rows.anchor: فإن المراد من الخلق إيجاد الشيء مقدرا تقديرا لا تفاوت فيه وهذا إنما يكون من الله سبحانه وتعالى

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سعد بن أبي سرح
rows.claim: A report says that when the Prophet dictated “another creation,” Ibn Abī Sarḥ anticipated “Blessed is God, the best of creators,” then claimed prophethood and defected to Mecca.
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن سعد بن أبي سرح كان يكتب لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فلما بلغ إلى قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says that, if the report is sound, this coincidence is not miraculous or impossible; Ibn Abī Sarḥ was confused or self-deceived by disbelief and envy.
rows.anchor: ولو صح هذا فإن هذا القدر لا يكون معجزا ولا يمتنع أن يتفق ذلك من الواحد منا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the completed formation, people die at their appointed time and are raised for the gathering, reckoning, and recompense.
rows.anchor: أي بعدما ذكرنا من تمام الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The body’s wondrously ordered construction ends in death for the sound purpose of resurrection; affirming the final resurrection does not deny other revivals.
rows.anchor: أخبر الله سبحانه أن هذه البنية العجيبة المبنية على أحسن إتقان وإحكام تنقض بالموت لغرض صحيح وهو البعث والإعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier revivals, including the thousands expelled from their homes and Moses’ people on the mountain, show that final resurrection does not exclude other revivals.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يمنع من الإحياء في القبور لأن إثبات البعث في القيامة لا يدل على نفي ما عداه ألا ترى أن الله سبحانه أحيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account contradicts al-Naẓẓām’s view that the human being is a spirit and Maʿmar’s view that a human is an indivisible, nonbodily thing.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دلالة على فساد قول النظام في أن الإنسان هو الروح وقول معمر إن الإنسان شيء لا ينقسم وإنه ليس بجسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven paths are seven heavens, each a path; they are called paths because they lie one above another.
rows.anchor: أي سبع سماوات كل سماء طريقة وسميت بذلك لتطارقها وهو أن بعضها فوق بعض

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī alternatively explains the paths as routes used by the angels.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لأنها طرائق الملائكة عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explains the paths as stacked layers, each layer being one path.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الطرائق الطباق وكل طبقة طريقة عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the distance between each pair of heavens, and between heaven and earth, is a journey of five hundred years.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن ما بين كل سمائين مسيرة خمسمائة عام وكذلك ما بين السماء والأرض عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says God was not heedless while building the heavens and placing the sun, moon, and stars in them.
rows.anchor: إذ بنينا فوقهم سبع سماوات أطلعنا فيها الشمس والقمر والكواكب

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says people were not created in vain: God created them knowing their actions and circumstances; this proves His knowledge of all things and warns against sin while encouraging obedience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه ما خلقناهم عبثا بل خلقناهم عالمين بأعمالهم وأحوالهم عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain is sent in a measure suited to need, not in excess that would ruin things and destroy them, but as welfare requires.
rows.anchor: أي بقدر الحاجة لا يزيد على ذلك فيفسد عنه فيهلك بل على ما توجبه المصلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gathers water into the earth for people’s benefit, preserving water in pools and sinkholes for summer when rain stops.
rows.anchor: أي جعلنا له الأرض مسكنا جمعناه فيه لينتفع به يريد ما يبقى في المستنقعات والدحلان أقر الله الماء فيها لينتفع الناس بها في الصيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istīnā is seeking familiarity through knowledge or another means; the Arab idiom “go and become familiar” means to find out whether anyone is there.
rows.anchor: الاستيناس طلب الأنس بالعلم أو غيره تقول العرب اذهب فاستأنس هل ترى أحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same verb appears in 4:6 with the sense “you know/perceive.”
rows.anchor: أي علمتم وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the wording should be “until you seek permission,” rather than “until you seek familiarity.”
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس أنه قال إنما هي تستأذنوا

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: A similar reading with “seek permission” is also transmitted from ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: وكذلك يروى عن عبد الله وروي عن أبي

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A reading transmitted from Ubayy puts greeting before seeking familiarity, and Ibn ʿAbbās is also said to have read it that way.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي حتى تسلموا وتستأنسوا وكذلك قرأ ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported to say that the written form is a scribal error and that the reading was “until you seek permission.”
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود وابن عباس قال أخطأ الكاتب فيه وكان يقرأ حتى تستأذنوا

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Another explanation takes istīnā as throat-clearing and speech that serve the function of asking permission, clarified by the rule for children reaching puberty.
rows.anchor: تستأنسوا بالتنحنح والكلام الذي يقوم مقام الاستيذان وقد بين الله تعالى ذلك في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك ومجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and al-Hasan take the bad and good things as words matched respectively with bad and good men.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس والضحاك ومجاهد والحسن

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd understands bad and good things as misdeeds and good deeds matched with bad and good men.
rows.anchor: من الرجال للطيبات من الحسنات عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم والجبائي
rows.claim: Abū Muslim and al-Jubbāʾī, as also transmitted from Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh, understand the verse as bad women for bad men and good women for good men.
rows.anchor: عن أبي مسلم والجبائي وهو المروي عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله ع

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh connect this marital reading to 24:2; some people wished to marry those women, but God disapproved and forbade it.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله ع قالا: هي مثل قوله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says “those” refers to the good people, who are cleared of the wicked speech.
rows.anchor: أي الطيبون مبرؤون أي منزهون من الكلام الخبيث عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ identifies them as ʿĀʾisha and Ṣafwān; the plural wording is used by grammatical predominance, as when a plural “siblings” includes two brothers.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: يعني به عائشة وصفوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good men and women receive God’s forgiveness for their sins and a generous gift in Paradise.
rows.anchor: أي لهؤلاء الطيبين من الرجال والنساء مغفرة من الله لذنوبهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās explain “seek familiarity” here as seeking permission before entering another person’s house.
rows.anchor: حتى تستأذنوا عن ابن مسعود وابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī connect the permission sense to the rule that children must ask permission when they reach puberty.
rows.anchor: وإذا بلغ الأطفال منكم الحلم فليستأذنوا [النور: 59] عن مجاهد والسدي

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب الأنصاري
rows.claim: Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī reports that the Prophet described announcing oneself with praise, glorification, or throat-clearing.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أيوب الأنصاري قال: " قلنا يا رسول الله ما الاستيناس قال:

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl ibn Saʿd reports that the Prophet warned a man who looked into his room, saying he would have jabbed his scratching tool into the man’s eye; permission exists because of sight.
rows.anchor: وعن سهل بن سعد قال " أطلع رجل في حجرة من حجر رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed man asked whether he must seek permission to enter on his mother; the Prophet said to do so, asking whether he wanted to see her naked.
rows.anchor: وروي أن " رجلا قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أستأذن على أمي فقال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing puts the actions in a different order: greet the residents, seek familiarity and permission, and enter only if allowed.
rows.anchor: قيل إن فيه تقديما وتأخيرا تقديره حتى تسلموا على أهلها وتستأنسوا وتستأذنوا فإن أذن لكم فادخلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, greeting itself creates familiarity; a man once cleared his throat at the Prophet’s door, so the Prophet had Rawḍa teach him to say, “Peace be upon you; may I enter?”
rows.anchor: فقد روي أن رجلا استأذن على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فتنحنح فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لامرأة يقال لها روضة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering after permission is better for visitors, who should remember God’s teachings, commands, and prohibitions and follow them.
rows.anchor: معناه ذلك الدخول بالاستيذان خير لكم

words: فَإِن لَّمْ تَجِدُوا۟ فِيهَآ أَحَدًۭا فَلَا تَدْخُلُوهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If no one is there to authorize entry, do not enter, since the house may contain things you may not see; a closed door also forbids peering in to find its occupants.
rows.anchor: معناه فإن لم تعلموا { فيها أحدا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s saying that permission exists because of sight grounds the rule against looking into a closed home; an open door, by contrast, permits looking.
rows.anchor: لقوله ع: " إنما جعل الاستيذان لأجل النظر " وإلا أن يكون الباب مفتوحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If residents tell visitors to leave, directly or by an evident signal, visitors must turn back rather than press their way in.
rows.anchor: أي فانصرفوا ولا تلجوا عليهم وذلك بأن يأمروكم بالانصراف صريحا أو يوجد منهم ما يدل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving is more beneficial in religion and worldly life, purer for the heart, and more likely to make visitors morally pure.
rows.anchor: معناه أن الانصراف أنفع لكم في دينكم ودنياكم وأطهر لقلوبكم وأقرب إلى أن تصيروا أزكياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no sin in entering uninhabited houses without permission when they contain something useful to visitors.
rows.anchor: أي حرج وإثم { أن تدخلوا بيوتا غير مسكونة } يعني بغير استئذان

rows.speaker: الصادق ومحمد بن الحنفية وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq, Muhammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, and Qatāda identify these houses as inns, bathhouses, and open courtyards, where visitors seek enjoyment or use.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أنها الحانات والحمامات والأرحبة عن الصادق ع وعن محمد ابن الحنفية وقتادة

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says they are abandoned ruins that a person enters to relieve himself.
rows.anchor: أنها الخرابات المعطلة ويدخلها الإنسان لقضاء الحاجة عن عطاء

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the houses as shops and merchants’ premises where people’s goods are stored.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أنها الحوانيت وبيوت التجار التي فيها أمتعة الناس عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says merchants’ bringing their goods to these places and making them available to people constitutes permission.
rows.anchor: جاءوا ببيوعهم فجعلوها فيها وقالوا للناس علموا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the houses are travelers’ stopping places where they take rest.
rows.anchor: والرابع: أنها مناخات الناس في أسفارهم يرتفقون بها عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers including all of the reported kinds of uninhabited public or useful places.
rows.anchor: والأولى حمله على الجميع { والله يعلم ما تبدون وما تكتمون } لا يخفى عليه شيء

words: وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ مَا تُبْدُونَ وَمَا تَكْتُمُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what people disclose and what they conceal; nothing is hidden from Him.
rows.anchor: لا يخفى عليه شيء من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The entry rule follows the emphatic condemnation of fornication and slander, keeping people farther from suspicion and closer to innocence from sin.
rows.anchor: وجه اتصال الآية بما قبلها أنه سبحانه لما عظم شأن الزنا والقذف أكد ذلك بالنهي عن دخول بيوت الناس

rows.speaker: البرجمي
rows.claim: Al-Barjamī reads the verb with an open nūn; the other readers use a ḍamma.
rows.anchor: قرأ البرجمي نسقيه بفتح النون والباقون نسقيه بضم النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference between the two readings of “We give to drink” was explained earlier.
rows.anchor: قد مضى الفرق بين نسقي ونسقى فيما تقدم

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: In an anomalous reading, al-Aʿraj reads “the sun” (al-ilāha) for “his god.”
rows.anchor: وفي الشواذ قراءة الأعرج من اتخذ الألاهة هواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ilāha means the sun; the form alāha with ḍamma is indeclinable, and the cited poem uses al-alāha for the sun.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ألهة بالضم غير مصروفة وأنشد: تروحنا من اللعباء عصرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading “and your deity” can mean your worship; it may also mean the sun worshipped by the addressee, like saying “your sun.”
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ وألهتك فمعناه وعبادتك وقد يجوز أن يكون أراد هذه المعرفة فأضافها إليه لعبادته لها

rows.speaker: ابن السميفع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfa reads “the winds, glad tidings” with the word bushran.
rows.anchor: وقراءة ابن السميفع الرياح بشرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bushran is a verbal noun used circumstantially, meaning “bearing good news,” like the idioms “hurry along continuously” and “they come to you running.”
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بشرى فهو مصدر وضع موضع الحال أي مبشرة كقولهم هلم جرا أي جارا أو منجرا ويأتينك سعيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers to his earlier discussion of the readers’ disagreement and proofs in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكرنا الاختلاف بين القراء فيه وما لهم من الاحتجاج في كل وجه منه في سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author also refers readers to an earlier discussion of the variant concerning “so that they may remember” in Sūrat Banī Isrāʾīl.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا اختلافهم في ليذكروا في سورة بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qabḍ means gathering parts that had been extended.
rows.anchor: القبض جمع الأجزاء المنبسطة واليسير السهل القريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yasīr can mean easy or near; it is also the opposite of difficult.
rows.anchor: واليسير السهل القريب واليسير أيضا نقيض العسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aysara describes a man who acquired enough wealth to make his affairs manageable.
rows.anchor: وأيسر الرجل ملك من المال ما تتيسر به الأمور عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation calls the left hand al-yusrā because it makes work easier with the right; tayāsara means to turn left.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اليد اليسرى لأنه يتيسر بها العمل مع اليمنى وتياسر أخذ في جهة اليد اليسرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subāt means cessation of work: one may say “he shaved his head,” and Saturday is named as the day work ceased.
rows.anchor: والسبات قطع العمل ومنه سبت رأسه سبتا إذا حلقه ومنه يوم السبت وهو يوم قطع العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nashr is the opposite of folding.
rows.anchor: والنشر خلاف الطي وأناسي جمع إنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anāsī is a plural of insān, with yāʾ replacing nūn; anāsīn is also said, and it may instead pluralize ansī like kursī/karāsī.
rows.anchor: وأناسي جمع إنسان جعلت الياء عوضا من النون وقد قالوا أيضا أناسين وقد يجوز أيضا أن يكون جمع أنسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause omits its pronoun because of its length: “the one whom God sent”; rasūlan is a circumstantial accusative attached to the omitted pronoun.
rows.anchor: العائد من الصلة إلى الموصول محذوف لطول الكلام أي بعثه الله رسولا منصوب على الحال من الهاء المحذوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In is lightened from inna with its subject omitted, understood as the affair; the lām in li-yuḍillanā emphasizes the predicate.
rows.anchor: وإن كان ليضلنا إن مخففة واسمه محذوف تقديره إنه كان وهو ضمير الأمر والشأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayfa may be a circumstantial accusative describing the implied subject of “extended,” or a verbal noun asking what kind of extension occurred.
rows.anchor: كيف في محل النصب على الحال من الضمير المستكن في مد والتقدير أمبدعا مد الظل أم لا ويجوز أن يكون في موضع المصدر

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says “Have you not seen?” is best taken as seeing with the heart, though seeing with the eyes is also possible.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: الأجود أن يكون " ألم تر " من رؤية القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under all readings, bushran is circumstantial, modifying “the winds” with arsala as its governing verb.
rows.anchor: وبشرا نصب على الحال في الوجوه كلها من الرياح والعامل فيه أرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional phrase “from what We created” functions as a circumstantial expression.
rows.anchor: مما خلقنا الجار والمجرور في موضع نصب على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the unbelievers see Muhammad, they only mock and belittle him, sarcastically asking whether this is the messenger God sent to them.
rows.anchor: أي وإذا شاهدوك يا محمد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the unbelievers’ claim as saying Muhammad nearly diverted them from worshipping their idols.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: معناه لقد كاد يصرفنا عن عبادة آلهتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here to lead astray means to take someone onto a road that ends in destruction.
rows.anchor: فإن الإضلال الأخذ بالشيء إلى طريق الهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied consequence is that, if they had not persevered in idol worship, they would have abandoned it.
rows.anchor: أي على عبادتها لأزلنا عن ذلك وحذف الجواب لدلالة الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God threatens the mockers with the punishment they will see plainly in the Hereafter, when it will be clear whether they or the believers were more astray.
rows.anchor: وسوف يعلمون حين يرون العذاب } الذي ينزل بهم في الآخرة عيانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth explanation takes “necks” as leaders or groups; in Arabic, “a neck of people came” means a group arrived.
rows.anchor: ورابعها: أن المراد بالأعناق الرؤساء والجماعات يقال جاءني عنق من الناس أي جماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth explanation assigns rational beings’ behavior to the necks because they have been described with an intelligent trait; a poetic line about the stars is cited.
rows.anchor: وخامسها: أنه لما وصف الأعناق بصفة ما يعقل نسب إليها ما يكون من العقلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The excerpt also preserves a poetic line comparing years taking something from the speaker to the dark portion of the moon, but gives no poet or gloss.
rows.anchor: أرى مر السنين أخذن مني كما أخذ السرار من الهلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poem describes the sons of Naʿsh (stars) inclining downward, illustrating language that treats nonhuman things like rational beings.
rows.anchor: تمرزتها والديك صباحه إذا ما بنو نعش دنوا فتصوبوا

rows.speaker: أبو حمزة الثمالي
rows.claim: Abū Ḥamza al-Thumālī says the verse concerns a voice from heaven in mid-Ramaḍān, after which young women come out of their houses.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو حمزة الثمالي في هذه الآية أنها صوت من السماء في النصف من شهر رمضان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse concerns his people and the Umayyads: his side will eventually rule, and their stubborn necks will submit and soften.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: نزلت فينا وفي بني أمية قال سيكون لنا عليهم الدولة فتخضع لنا أعناقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each newly arriving reminder from the Merciful is a fresh Qur’anic revelation, yet the unbelievers turn away without reflecting on it.
rows.anchor: أي جديد يعني القرآن كما قال إنا نحن نزلنا الذكر وإنا له لحافظون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since they have rejected the reminder, the realities of what they mocked will reach them later, on the Day of Resurrection; the author points to Sūrat al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: فيما بعد يعني يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A pair or kind means a type together with its counterpart; karīm can mean beautiful.
rows.anchor: معناه من كل نوع معه قرينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other glosses take karīm as beneficial and praiseworthy, or as a kind prized by the people who use it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نافع محمود مما يحتاج إليه. وقيل: من كل صنف يكرم على أهله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says karīm refers to every kind of plant that people and livestock eat.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كريم مما يأكل الناس والأنعام عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says people are plants of the earth, citing the statement that God made humanity grow from the earth; those in Paradise are noble and those in Hell lowly.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: الناس نبات الأرض كما قال سبحانه والله أنبتكم من الأرض نباتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flourishing variety of plants is a sign of God’s oneness and the completeness of His power.
rows.anchor: أي لدلالة على وحدانيتنا وكمال قدرتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people do not believe or acknowledge the sign, out of obstinacy, imitation of their forebears, and avoidance of the burden of religious obligation.
rows.anchor: أي لا يصدقون بذلك ولا يعترفون به عنادا وتقليدا لأسلافهم وهربا من مشقة التكليف

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh treats kāna as extra here, making the expression equivalent to “most of them did not believe.”
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه كان هنا مزيدة ومجازه وما أكثرهم مؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is al-ʿAzīz, powerful and never overcome, and al-Raḥīm, who bestows many kinds of favor on His servants.
rows.anchor: أي القادر والذي لا يعجز والغالب الذي لا يغلب { الرحيم } أي المنعم على عباده

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb reads “and my breast tightens” and “my tongue does not speak” in the accusative; the other readers use the nominative.
rows.anchor: قرأ يعقوب ويضيق ولا ينطلق بالنصب فيهما والباقون بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative readings coordinate with “I fear”; the accusative readings coordinate with “that they may deny me.”
rows.anchor: من قرأ يضيق ولا ينطلق بالرفع عطف على أخاف ومن قرأ بالنصب عطف على أن يكذبون

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسلم بن يسار وحماد بن سلمة
rows.claim: In a noncanonical reading, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Yasār and Ḥammād ibn Salama read the address with tāʾ: “Will you not be God-fearing?”
rows.anchor: وفي الشواذ قراءة عبد الله بن مسلم بن يسار وحماد بن سلمة ألا تتقون بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tāʾ reading supplies an unspoken “say to them,” making the words Moses’ direct address to Pharaoh’s people.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ ألا تتقون بالتاء فهو على إضمار القول أي فقل لهم ألا تتقون

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī has a variant reading of the phrase referring to Moses’ deed.
rows.anchor: التاء وقراءة الشعبي وفعلت فعلتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With kasra on the first fāʾ, faʿla is like rukba or jalsa and names a state or manner; this pattern can also be a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ فعلتك بكسر الفاء فهي مثل الركبة والجلسة تكون كناية عن الحال التي يكون عليها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses “when” as an accusative dependent on an omitted command to recount the story, supported by the following instruction to tell Abraham’s story.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: موضع إذ نصب على معنى واتل عليهم هذه القصة فيما تتلو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to go to the unjust people is the object of “called,” as the message Moses was called to deliver.
rows.anchor: موضعه نصب بأنه مفعول نادى أي ناداه بهذه الكلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular form “messenger” may convey a plural meaning, or each of Moses and Aaron may be individually called a messenger.
rows.anchor: رسول رب العالمين واحد في معنى الجمع كقوله فإنهم عدو لي ويجوز أن يكون كل واحد منهما رسولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may be nominative as an appositive to “favor,” or accusative as its cause: Pharaoh’s enslavement of Israel made Moses’ survival seem a favor.
rows.anchor: إن عبدت بني إسرائيل في موضع رفع لأنه بدل من نعمة تقديره وتلك نعمة تعبيدك بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the causative parsing, Pharaoh’s act becomes a “favor” only ironically: without his persecution, Moses’ family would have kept and protected him instead of casting him into the river.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون في موضع نصب بأنه مفعول له أي إنما صارت نعمة لأن عبدت بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In one parsing, mā is nominative and dhā is a relative pronoun, giving “what thing do you command?”
rows.anchor: فماذا تأمرون يجوز أن يكون ما في موضع رفع بالابتداء وذا بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, mā is the object and mādhā functions as one compound interrogative, “what do you advise?”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون في موضع نصب بأنه مفعول تأمرون ويكون مع ذا بمنزلة اسم واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stories of earlier messengers console Muhammad and urge him to persevere, trusting that victory will come.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر سبحانه أقاصيص رسله تسلية للرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وتحريضا له على الصبر ثقة بنزول النصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tells Muhammad to recount the time the Creator called Moses and ordered him to go to people who sinned against themselves and oppressed Israel with severe punishment.
rows.anchor: أي واذكر يا محمد واتل عليهم الوقت الذي نادى فيه ربك الذي خلقك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pharaoh’s people” is an explanatory apposition to “the unjust people.”
rows.anchor: ثم بين القوم الموصوفين بهذه الصفة فقال: { قوم فرعون } وهو عطف بيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported third-person wording means, “Is it not time for them to fear?” and avoid God’s punishment through obedience.
rows.anchor: إنما قاله بالياء لأنه على الحكاية ومعناه أما آن لهم أن يتقوا ويصرفوا عن أنفسهم عقوبة الله بطاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā means avoiding reprehensible things by doing good; its root sense is to put a barrier between oneself and what one avoids.
rows.anchor: والتقوى مجانبة القبائح بفعل المحاسن وأصله صرف الأمر بحاجز بين الصارف وبينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses fears that Pharaoh’s people will deny his message and refuse to accept it; fear is the soul’s agitation at an expected event, unlike the soul’s settled security.
rows.anchor: بالرسالة ولا يقبلوا مني والخوف انزعاج النفس بتوقيع ونقيضه الأمن
